Mr. Speaker, Bill C-171 is a relatively short bill. The commodities to which it refers have long since been forgotten by members of this House. Actually, many members of the House never knew of the proposals in the budget which gave rise to these changes. These changes are limited to those that the minister announced in the budget of May 8, 1972. Basically they cover a limited number of commodities on which taxes have either been eliminated or on which they are to be reduced.
Before I deal with the particular provisions of the bill which apply to such things as, contact lenses, crates used

in transportation, eel traps and a few things like that, I should like to say that the House, I am sure, was very disappointed that even in his last budget address the minister did not announce that there was being undertaken a general review of the entire sales tax, as that applies to the government of Canada. We know that the Carter Commission made some proposals about the whole question, but we have not heard anything about them for seve.-al months. I will wait until the minister pays attention.
He is not paying attention to you.
Perhaps I could have the attention of both hon. gentlemen who are now conferring, since they are the ones to whom I should like to make these remarks.
Send the minister a letter, Marcel.

An hon. member suggests that I should send a letter. It would never get there on time. I am not satisfied that the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) could get it there on time.
The point I was hoping to impress on the minister, and on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if he had stayed in the chamber, is the necessity of a total review of the sales tax provisions that apply at the federal level. Over the years the act has become a mishmash of parts that were repealed, of additions, and of many schedules that are a jungle of inconsistencies. Actually, there is in my mind a very grave question about the efficacy of flat rate consumption taxes. These are imposed on an ad valorem basis. As prices rise, the revenues of the government rise. The federal sales tax is a regressive tax in that it hits more heavily-

That, however, does not alter the fact that leadership for a total review of consumption taxes, such as sales taxes, must be given in this country if tax reform is to have any meaning. If the subject of tax reform in this country has been abandoned by the Liberal administration because it has exhausted in producing the new Income Tax Act, I can readily understand the apparent lack of progress. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is talking now about a guaranteed annual income. This administration more and more seems to be moving in that direction, even though the Prime Minister in 1968 had rejected the whole idea. Before there can be any element of justice with regard to a guaranteed annual income, the question of sales and consumption taxes at both federal and provincial sales levels must be considered.
Having said that, I should like to ask the minister to say what steps have been taken since his predecessor many months ago indicated that this action was to be organized. when we consider the bill in committee of the whole. I will talk about certain principles underlying this bill. After we have heard from representatives in the House, I hope that we will move into committee of the whole to deal with the particular points.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) I; too, intend to be very brief in speaking on Bill C-171. This bill also deals with legislation proposed in the budget of last year. It removes the sales tax from a number of items which help people such as farmers. In my area, this measure will be helpful because it removes the sales tax on crates for live poultry. After all, Yorkton is the turkey capital of the world. Therefore, I enthusiastically support this part of the legislation. In answer to the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), I maintain that Yorkton is the turkey capital, not the Fraser Valley. This bill exempts a whole series of items from sales tax such as chicken and turkey crates, eyeglasses, contact lenses and so on.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). He questioned the wisdom of sales taxes in general and asked the government to review the idea of a sales tax because it is regressive. I agree that sales tax is extremely regressive. I wonder what the Progressive Conservative party thinks about the Ontario government which yesterday implemented a 7 per cent sales tax across the board.
What about Saskatchewan where it started?

In Saskatchewan, the sales tax is now 5 per cent. In Ontario, it is 7 per cent, one of the highest in the country. That really indicates where the hearts of the generous Tories are when it comes to the average citizen. It strikes me as funny to hear the hon. member for Edmonton West question the wisdom of sales tax and suggest that it is regressive when his own party in the province of Ontario is increasing the sales tax.
Shame.

I say sincerely that sales tax is regressive. It is imposed across the board and hurts in particular those in the lower and middle income groups. The sales tax in this country should be lowered rather than increased, such as is being done in Ontario. Therefore, I support the bill before us. I am happy to see that a number of items are now being exempted from sales tax. The clause dealing with eyeglasses, contact lenses and other items connected with eye problems is worth-while. The clause dealing with crates for live poultry is very worthwhile, especially in an area like mine, as are other clauses in the bill.
The only question I want to raise at this time concerns providing more exemptions for mining companies in the exploration and drilling for oil and gas. I again want to make the point that the government is handing out another tax exemption to the resource and extractive industries. These industries are already receiving a lot of tax. breaks. They are capital intensive. They do not provide jobs. We

should look in the opposite direction, plug some of the loopholes and increase taxation for the mining and oil companies. This would entice more money into the manufacturing industry as well as the development of service industries which in turn, would provide more jobs for the people of this country.
The hon. member for Edmonton West may think this rather frivolous. I understand his thinking. He represents, in a very profound way, the thinking of the economic neanderthals of the Conservative party in Alberta, the people who represent the oil and gas companies in this country. What we need in this country is a real change in the tax policy regarding the extractive industries. It is time we did more processing of raw materials in this country. There should be more development in this area. If we did that, we probably would not have the high rate of unemployment that we have today.
In conclusion, we will support the measure before us. During the committee stage, one or two members of this party may have a question or two for the minister.

Mr. Speaker, the bill now under consideration will surely encourage a few sectors of the economic activity in Canada and will not do much for others, while the federal government is on the verge, as an hon. member pointed out a while ago, of abolishing the sales tax on certain drug products and certain other items to help large families. However, at the same time, we hear about tax increases at the provincial level. For example, the Ontario government announced last night that the sales tax would go up from 5 to 7 per cent, while it already stands at 8 per cent in Quebec.
And the Sacreds in British Columbia raised it to 6 per cent.
And the Conservatives in British Columbia have raised it to 6 per cent.
No. The Conservatives are not in power; it is an NDP government.

The New Democratic Party is in power. In Alberta where the Conservatives are in power, there is talk of a soon to be established sales tax and the hon. member for Edmonton West will probably soon have to confirm it.
Mr. Speaker, oil reserves are all being devoured in Alberta since the Conservatives took over.
The sales tax hits directly big families which naturally have to buy more than small families. Big families are usually those with low incomes; they are the families hardest hit by tax increases in Ontario. But it is not up to the Minister of Finance to tell the government of Ontario not to impose taxes.
This morning I heard the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (M. Douglas) ask with respect to the tax on gasoline or the 2 cent increase in the price of gasoline if the federal government intended to do anything about it.
Mr. Speaker, I was tempted to ask a question at that time to see if in 1944 when the hon. member for Nanaimo-

Cowichan-The Islands was premier of Saskatchewan, the tax on gasoline was removed. Was private entreprise not taxed? For example, were there not oil companies which refused to settle in Saskatchewan because they feared they might be nationalized or controlled by the government? Those are questions which might have been asked this morning had the hon. member been a minister in this government. It may soon come true judging from the way we see the New Democratic Party walk hand in hand with this government. What is now held against the government was applied in Saskatchewan not too long ago and it is still being applied today.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a solution to say: you are blamed for imposing such a tax while everybody is asking for better services in all fields; everybody, especially the New Democratic Party, is clamouring for assistance, as did a while ago the member for Winnipeg North Centre (M. Knowles) who spoke about public servants who. should be granted a pension raise, etc. We agree. Why should they get higher pensions? To have more purchasing power!
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, we are drawing those increases from the pockets of the taxpayers; we reduce the purchasing power of the general consumer to help a certain class of society. Help a group of citizens, fair enough, but not at the expense of another which is sometimes poorer than the one we are trying to help.
Mr. Speaker, changing the taxation procedure is not new; it has been invented, not by the government, nor by the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands nor by myself, but by economists who say that the tax basis should be better distributed in order to reach a given social class.
Mr. Speaker, whether they be Liberals, Progressive Conservatives or New Democrats, most economists have studied in the same universities, yet they contradict each other and confuse governments instead of enlightening them.
I do have a grudge against such economist who dwell in the clouds, get lost in the fog and want to distribute taxation through additionnal bureaucracy, which means more administration expenses and fewer services than ever before.
Mr. Speaker, this is why me should not always rely on taxation; from time to time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) says; the only way to get money is to tax or borrow. How empty those words sound, coming from a sovereign government! It does not enjoy sovereignty; then, where does it find sovereignty? In taxation and borrowing. But why does sovereign government, strong legal and able in a country such as Canada find itself unable to create the credit it needs to serve the people?
Mr. Sepaker, after getting up in the morning and saying the "Lord's Prayer" and the a "Hail, Mary", the Minister of Finance should learn by heart the statement made by Abraham Lincoln in the 1860's when he was President of the United States. This would complement his prayers.

I have two great enemies-the southern army in front of me and the financial institutions in the rear. Of the two, the one behind me is my greatest foe. The government should create,-

The Minister of Finance is looking at me; these words are not mine but those of Abraham Lincoln; the minister willingly follows the example of this great stateman in other fields, but not in the financial field. No, we must not talk about that.
I resume the quotation:

-the government should create, issue and circulate all the currency required to satisfy the spending power of the government and the buying power of consumers.

The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Island has used the same words in western Canada. In 1934-35, the hon. member drove in Saskatchewan in a 1929 model car; I saw the picture. On the one hand, he was saying: Vote CCF, and on the other hand he was saying: Vote Social Credit. At the time of William Eberhart, he almost became a member of the Social Credit Party.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member none the less recognizes that he used Abraham Lincoln's words.
Was he not a student that time?

He was not a student but I must admit he was very clever. Only when he joined the ranks of the CCF did he lose some of his ability.
Mr. Speaker, Abraham Lincoln said, and I quote: [English]
The privilege of creating and issuing money is not only the supreme prerogative of government-
[ Translation]
I hope the Minister of Finance understands. I go on quoting:

-it is the government's greatest creative opportunity. [Translation]
Is the hon. member suggesting that he was an advocate of Social Credit?

No, but I can say that I agree with him. I wish the minister would agree with him as well. If he did and undertook exactly what Abraham Lincoln suggested, the minister might conclude by saying: At last, that is Social Credit!

The people can and will be furnished with a currency as safe as their own country. Money will cease to be master and become the servant of the people. Democracy will rise superior to the money power.

Those were the words of Abraham Lincoln. When will the Minister of Finance start saying and repeating those words and, above all, putting them into effect? I am looking forward to that. The sipritual leader of the present Minister of Finance was the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. That is true!
That is tough!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. May I remind the hon. member that we are considering a specific bill, Bill C-171, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act. I assume that the remarks of the hon. member are introductory to his statement, but I hope that he will soon come to the subject matter of the bill now before us.

Mr. Speaker, I am quoting the former president of the United States Abraham Lincoln, and one former Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, because they were definitely opposed to this excise tax which is dealt with in Bill C-171.
This tax is to a high degree responsible for inflation in Canada; even if we abolish the tax on candies and on some drugs, it will not do much to improve the financial situation.
Let us take, for example, the effects of excise tax in the field of automobiles. Mr. Speaker, I am an automobile salesman. On a $4,000 car, the excise tax is just under $300; the federal sales tax comes to between $500 and $700 and on top of that there is the provincial tax. What an agglomeration of taxes-
They benefit the salesman!

An hon. member says: "They benefit the salesman"! Mr. Speaker, if our profits were that much, we would be rich. Then we would be able to pay more income tax! The excise and other taxes on automobiles and other products are enough. We should at least have exemption from the provincial sales tax.
To come back to what I was saying just now, I know that the Right Hon. Mackenzie King is not behind Bill C-171, but his spirit is there. The Minister of Finance could abolish the excise tax on a number of products if he took the advice of his "spiritual father".
I quote again:

Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and democracy is idle and futile.
Mr. Speaker, it was a Liberal prime minister of Canada who made such a statement in 1935, nearly forty years ago. And today, we still have to deal with the same system. Taxes are distributed instead of abundance. We forget the products which exist in Canada; we still hear stupid

economists say that there is not enough production in relation to the purchasing power, while exactly the opposite is true. Today, in order to stimulate employment, they say that private enterprise is going to be subsidized, that the excise tax will be removed on some items, holding out to the people the prospect of an increase in the purchasing power and of new jobs.
Yesterday evening, I saw the advertisement for 300,000 jobs. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was wrong as usual and advertised three million jobs. The bureaucrats who do not even have enough time to think what figures they must write down are as strong as 10 years ago. They are irresponsible, as usual.
Mr. Speaker, 300,000 jobs will be created by the Minister of Finance, but they do not say how many new Canadians will join the labour market. The 300,000 jobs of the Minister of Finance remind me of the 100,000 jobs of Mr. Bou-rassa, in the province of Quebec, where 100,000 jobs became 100,000 layoffs. There are more unemployed in the province of Quebec than at the time when Mr. Bourassa came to power in 1970, and at the national level, there are more unemployed than 3 or 4 years ago. This is the result of such a system! They think that they will improve the well-being of Canadians by giving goodies.
Moreover, automation is increasing every day and shows that we need less and less labour, and human capital. What is needed is automatic capital and I would like the Minister of Finance to find automatic financial capital. Financial capital must work as automation does and then the excise tax would not have to be abolished or altered since the minister would have found a concrete solution. We want to get the economy moving again. There is only one way of making it work: we must increase the consumers' buying power without increasing prices. This is the only way. We will not succeed through the excise tax but through the Bank of Canada and by compensated retail price discounts.
The federal government could use the Bank of Canada so this would not be reflected in prices and in production costs; by decreasing consumption prices, compensated by the federal government, by the Bank of Canada or by a national credit commission, the products would reach consumers and create new jobs through increased demand. Those products would then be made in Canada and not in Japan or Jamaica.
The abolition of the excise tax on certain products is only a drop of water in the ocean. This is not a solution to the problem and if the other parties are happy with that, we are not. We will of course accept the removal of the excise tax on certain products, but this is not enough and the Minister of Finance knows it.
Therefore, I wish, as I said earlier, that in addition to saying his "Hail Mary" or his "Our Father", morning and night, the minister should learn by heart what Abraham Lincoln said in the United States, so that we may establish in Canada a system respectful of all citizens.

I have had one or two questions about this asked of me, and I should like to have an understanding that section 1 does, in fact, include an exemption for gill nets, seine nets or trawl nets. I ask this question because one reads down through this part into Nos. 2, 3, 4, etc., certain specific things are spelled out in detail, but nowhere in the present bill are nets of any kind specifically mentioned. That answers that question. Would the specific amendment contained in Bill C-171, which has to do with the amendment to No. 4, cover this? As I understand it, this is an attempt to close a gap which has existed in the details of exempt items, possibly because of the development of new kinds of fisheries. I wonder whether the general intent is to exempt all of the items required to engage in a commercial fishery, and whether this form of dealing with it is necessarily the best one. The section would include traps and pots used for catching lobsters, crab and shrimp and the proposal is to add cod traps and eel traps.
The question occurred to me immediately, what about the prawn fishery? If one is going to go into that kind of detail, is it necessary for someone engaged in the prawn fishery, as distinct from the shrimp fishery, to go through the rather exhaustive process of making representations to the government in order to find out that a particular type of gear which may be used is exempt? As I understand this part of the section, it is the gear not attached to or necessarily part of the regular equipment of the boat that is exempt. Must this happen every time some new form of fishery is developed and, if so, has consideration been given to what I might describe as a more generic approach being taken, setting out these items? Can the minister shed light on this question?

We have a serious problem here but, as is customary, parliament likes to have a review of specific items with amendments on the floor of the House. There is a different method of looking after people who are mentally retarded. They are no longer locked up in institutions or, shall we say, confined to mental institutions. This has reference to the blind and the deaf and dumb, but what is being done about the physically handicapped?

I rise on a point of order. I wonder if I might help the hon. member by referring him to the later ways and means resolution which I tabled on February 19 of this year, in which there is a further amendment proposed to this part of the schedule to include goods produced by the labour of individuals who are in any other manner mentally or physically handicapped.

All right, that meets part of the question. That meets the part in respect of the physically handicapped, but I am talking about the sheltered workshops which exist throughout the country where we have those who are not severely retarded. I am referring to people who do not live in an institution but live in a home and go to a sheltered workshop. This is not covered under this particular amendment.
It is.

It is not covered unless the minister is referring to the February one. I do not have it before me. I thank the minister for reminding me what he did in February. I am referring to the sheltered workshops and also the rehabilitation centres.
That is in the February one.

That is good. I think this will shorten the debate a good deal. A number of my colleagues were concerned about this. This is part and parcel of the difficulties of the dog's breakfast type of budget proposals we have to consider.
Now I shall come to the sales outlets. We have a series of shops in Edmonton known as the Marina shops. They handle goods made exclusively by a group of handicapped persons, and are the sole outlets for these products. Naturally sales amount to more than $3,000 a year and therefore Marina does not have the small manufacturers' license. Incidentally, while on that point I hope the minister will do something about the $3,000 limit on a small manufacturers' license. That should have gone out the window ten years ago because the limitation of $3,000 for total output in a year is ridiculous. It was ridiculous ten years ago and now is even more so. These outlets to which I am referring are not for private gain. The proceeds are strictly for the benefit of the handicapped persons whose goods go through these shops. However, the goods handled by these outlets are subject to sales tax. There is much correspondence on file relative to this. Through participation of the province of Alberta, also grants from the government of Canada, and much private help, this major research and training institution for the physically handicapped was established. I have been there. They do a great deal of printing, monotonous and repetitious work. However, this is exclusively for the training of mentally handicapped persons and so on.
This is a program for the development of human resources. I cannot make a strong enough plea for assistance in respect of this particular type of program. We have all sorts of development programs concerning agricultural land, resources and so on, but what do we actually do for the totality of human resources in this country? We have educational programs, training programs and retraining programs for all those people who are physically and mentally able. But what do we actually do for so many of

our mentally handicapped people? At one time these people were locked away in a closet. They were placed in institutions by the thousands to live a vegetable-like existence. Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank the House for its co-operation in passing the two prior bills so expeditiously. We are now on the third bill relating to the budgetary matters affecting the 1972 calendar year. Bill C-172 is an act to amend the Customs Tariff.
I think it would be fair to say that the most significant provisions of this bill are those relating to the establishment of a general preferential tariff for imports from developing countries. As I said in my budget speech last May, this measure is Canada's contribution to a global effort to help the developing countries improve their exports to world markets. This broad international initiative, known as the generalized system of preferences, has been endorsed by the United National General Assembly as an important element in the international development strategy for the second United Nations "Development Decade" which began in 1971.
Tariff preferences in favour of developing countries have been under discussion internationally for a number of years, beginning in 1964 at the first United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, UNCTAD. At that time a number of industrialized countries, including Canada and the United States, were not convinced that the creation of tariff preferences was an appropriate way of assisting the industrialization and economic developing countries. It seemed doubtful that the developing countries would obtain much more in the way or real benefits from a new preferential system than they would from continued progress towards trade liberalization on a multilateral or most-favoured-nation basis. Of course, not even the developing countries were under any illusion that tariff preferences would solve all their problems or obviate the need for more conventional forms of development assistance. These countries, and particularly the

April 13, 1973
Customs Tariff
Group of "77" in UNCTAD, were nevertheless convinced that tariff preferences offered them the best prospects for achieving better access to foreign markets, and hence increased exports and higher standards of living.
The issue became as much a political one as an enonomic one, and by the time of UNCTAD II in 1968, attitudes had changed to the point where the conference was able to reach unanimous agreement, in principle, to the early establishment of a system of generalized, non-reciprocal and non-discriminatory tariff preferences for the manufactured and semi-manufactured exports of the developing countries. The details of the system were left to be worked out at subsequent meetings and indeed it was not until the fall of 1970 that a mutually acceptable system was agreed upon in UNCTAD. The system in fact consists of a number of different preferential schemes, each reflecting the particular circumstances of the individual preference giving country. A common feature, however, is that they all contain safeguard provisions under which the preferential rates can be withdrawn when imports reach certain levels or threaten injury to domestic producers. Most of these preferential schemes have now been implemented, and indeed Canada and the United States are the only countries that have not brought their schemes into force.
The details of Canada's proposed new preferential tariff are set out in Clause 2 of the bill that is now before the House, but perhaps it would be useful if I were to summarize its main features. First, it will provide for lower tariffs on most manufactured and semi-manufactured goods imported from developing countries. Certain primary products are also covered by the scheme but these are for the most part already duty free on a mostfavoured-nation basis and so, of course, there is not the same scope for tariff reductions on them. The tariff reductions for industrial goods are spelled out in subsection (1) of proposed new section 3.1 of the Customs Tariff. Hon. members will note that general preferential tariff rates will be set at two thirds of the most-favoured-nation rate or at the level of the present British preferential rate, whichever is lower. This will mean free entry under many tariff items. It also means that the general preferential tariff will go a long way towards eliminating the discrimination that has existed in our tariff treatment of developing countries as between those that are members of the Commonwealth and those that are not.
Second, there will be tariff reductions on a selected list of agricultural products. These are set out in the schedule to subsection (3) of proposed new section 3.1 of the Customs Tariff.
A third feature of the new preferential system is the "safeguard" clause which will authorize the governor in council to withdraw the benefits of the general preferential tariff in particular cases. This will be used to deal with any case where imports at preferential rates cause or threaten market disruption or injury to Canadian producers. It is the government's intention to use this authority to exclude from the preferential system at the outset a limited number of sensitive products-mainly textile products for which we have negotiated export restraints or which have been placed under import control. When the legislation is proclaimed, a complete list of the

products to be excluded on this basis will be published by order in council.
Finally, the bill would authorize the governor in council to decide what countries should be considered to be developing countries for purposes of the new preferential system. Final decisions in this regard have still to be taken but, as a general rule, any country, area or territory entitled to MFN or BP tariff treatment which claims to be a developing country and which receives preferences from other preference-giving countries will be eligible under the Canadian scheme. Of course, we know what countries are eligible for the preferential schemes that have already been implemented.
None of the countries that have implemented their schemes has extended the preferences to all the countries that claim to be developing countries and some beneficiary lists are longer than others. Most of the members of the so-called Group of "77" developing countries, who now apparently number 97, are receiving preferences under the schemes that have been implemented and dependent territories are also eligible for several of them. However, there is considerably less unanimity as to whether the preferences should be extended to such countries as Spain, Portugal, Greece, Turkey, Taiwan, Israel, Bulgaria and Roumania, all of which claim developing country status. Japan is the only donor country that has given preferences to all these countries.
It is of course difficult to estimate the volume of trade that will be affected by the Canadian scheme. If the preferences were extended to the 88 countries of the Group of "77" who are entitled to BP or MFN treatment, as well as to dependent territories, it is estimated that there would be tariff reductions on around $160 million worth of imports. This estimate is based on 1971 import statistics and does not, of course, include imports from Commonwealth developing countries under those tariff items where the general preferential tariff rate will be equal to the current BP rate. If this figure appears small, it should be borne in mind that close to 70 per cent of our imports from developing countries are already free of duty.
There are three other amendments I should like to mention at this time. The first relates to two textile items in the schedule to the Bill. The British preferential rate for rubber coated woven cord tire fabric under item 56235-1 is increased from free to the 12 VS per cent rate which applies under the most-favoured-nation tariff. The duty on knit goods from Britain is increased from a net rate of 18 per cent to 25 per cent under tariff item 56805-1. Both these proposed increases follow upon the implementation by Britain on January 1, 1972 of increased rates of duty on cotton textiles from Canada. These Canadian goods were previously entitled to free entry. The tariff increases which have been the subject of negotiations with the British government were intended to restore the balance of concessions with Britain.
The second change arises out of a Tariff Board decision in May, 1971 on an appeal relating to tariff item 69605-1. This item provides for free entry of certain goods for the use of religious and educational institutions. As a result of the Tariff Board decision, the coverage of the item was considerably reduced. The amendment to item 69605-1 will restore its scope to approximately what it was formerly.
April 13, 1973

Customs Tariff
The third change is also the result of a Tariff Board ruling on an appeal. The Board held that live yeast in granular form should be dutiable at an MFN rate lower than had been levied by the Department of National Revenue under tariff items which provided for "compressed yeast". Representations were received from Canadian producers of yeast stating that the Board's decision would have a serious impact on their operations. On the other hand, it was argued that the previous rates were too high. The proposed item 3600-1 will provide for a 121/2 per cent MFN rate on live yeast, irrespective of the form in which it is imported.
Those are the main features in terms of importance of the bill and, certainly, when we come to the clause-byclause analysis in committee I will be glad to expend upon that.

Mr. Speaker, the minister having made a fairly detailed explanation of a fairly short customs budgetary amendment, I do not think it is necessary for me to dwell at length on the contents of this bill or on the principles involved in its presentation and consideration. I will repeat what I said when Bill C-171 was considered. It is anti-climactic to deal with this particular bill now. It is 11 months since the budgetary proposals were made. At least half the members of this House have never heard of them, and I suppose most of the others have more or less forgotten what the minister proposed. Actually, I do not suppose anybody in this House outside of a small handful have ever known of a class of tariffs known as General Preferential Tariffs.
The minister indicated that there is to be considerable relief for some of the developing countries. I am not too sure about that suggestion, especially when I look at clause 2 which establishes the general preferential tariff. Subclause (2) of Clause 2 reads in part:
The following goods are excluded from the application of subsection (1):
(a) the goods enumerated in any of the tariff items in Groups I,
II, III, IV and VI of Schedule A . . .
I have before me most of the customs Tariff and the five groups that come under Schedule A comprise the bulk of the tariff. Some exceptions are noted; one is a classical one. Let me refer to the first one that comes under item No. 1210-1, which appears under Part I. Why we are maintaining tariff protection with regard to this item I do not know. It is listed as "sausage casings, synthetic, of paper" and there is a 10 per cent and 15 per cent tariff on that. Somehow we have decided that we cannot import these types of sausage casings free of charge. We cannot extend to them the benefits of the general preferential tariff. There are other things that appear in the tariff, and I know some are of greater strategical importance than others. One sees, on examining this, that there is a reduction to zero under the general preferential tariff with regard to a number of things that one associates with, shall we say, developing countries. Sometimes Canada, for certain purposes, decides that it is a developing country. In terms of our relationship with the United States and our capital requirements, we seem to think we are a developing country.
The free entry of such things as chicory, pepper, cloves, cinnamon, ginger, spices, and spices, nutmegs and mace, nutmegs and mace ground, ground mustard, rice meal, sago and tapioca, fruits and nuts, preserved ginger and coconut loom very large. They have been reduced to zero. Frankly, that is because the rate that would be left would only be 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent. Even unstemmed and stemmed Turkish tobacco comes in at zero rate under the general preferential tariffs. Be that as it may, we do not have much more to say about these changes. We will have a great deal more to say when we are considering the proposals the minister made in February which will affect the horticultural industry and a number of other industries in this country. The sooner we have that bill before us and are able to discuss and clarify the matter, the better off we will be in this country. I do not know whether the minister puts this measure in the same category as some of the very touchy income tax subjects. At the moment, I think he is handling them with 10 foot or 20 foot poles. Which is it? The minister remains discreetly silent.
Are 20 foot poles tariff free?

At the present time, the clarifying items are of very little concern. One point we may hear more about is the adjustment vis-a-vis the British preferential tariff arising out of Britain's entry into the common market and Britain's necessary adjustment within that framework. When Britain removes certain preferential tariffs on Canadian commodities, it is only fair to expect that we will do the same. In many ways, I regret this. Lower rates mean a great deal. While events have changed, in many ways we are being left behind in this move. With Britain joining the European common market, we in Canada are standing aloof.
Reports from Europe indicate that the president of Mexico is having a considerable impact on the common market members in so far as Mexico is concerned in this issue. Mexico is in much the same position as Canada, only on the other side of the United States. However, the North American continent is a particular zone, merely three countries in so far as trading is concerned.
Canada should be endeavouring to present a very high profile in Europe vis-a-vis the common market countries today. No matter how good our ambassadors may be, they are still diplomatic representatives. This calls for the highest possible level of representation by Canadians, perhaps a full fledged policy tour this year by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of Canada, whoever he may be. The matter of trade relations with our European counterparts should be very seriously considered. There are no two ways about this; it has to be done. If I were to make this suggestion to the minister, I am sure he would admit that he doubts very much that the Prime Minister of Canada would be received in France with open arms at this stage, but something has to be done. The necessary steps must be taken to remove some of the underbrush, thaw some of the ice that exists and remove some of the slick patches on which people have slipped in the past. In so far as my advice to my leader is concerned, it would be and is that

April 13, 1973
Customs Tariff
Canada's presence at the very top level must be made in Europe.
This may be a bit removed from customs tariffs, but it is related to our trade relations with our partners. As a result of Britain's entry into the common market, we will be in an unsettled period for five, eight or 10 years. We should not sit in the reeds moaning and groaning or run to London or Paris cap in hand to beg for special consideration for a special position. If it takes the necessary steps at the top level, Canada will be in a position to broaden its trade. We need positive action. No one is going to help us. We have to help ourselves. The only way to do that is to go out and state our case. People in Europe are interested in trading with Canada, not merely for sentimental reasons, and we are interested in trading with them, not just for sentimental reasons, but because it is good for business. It is good for the economies of their country and ours.
That is all I want to say at this stage of the bill. When the next tariff bill is before us, we will have considerably more to say.

Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, we are very pleased to see a trend toward lower tariffs. It has been a long standing position of our party, that not only Canada, but the world should be moving towards less restricted trade patterns. It is natural that we in this party should be concerned about lower tariffs because of the large contingent of members from British Columbia and Saskatchewan who never cease to remind the caucus of the grievances of the western provinces.
Hear, hear!

As Your Honour will notice, a couple of western members have been appointed to keep their eye on me so that I will say the right things.
It is important that a country like Canada move in a direction of freer trade for two reasons. First, we have to be competitive in the world. The sooner we come to grips with competition around the world, the healthier it will be for our economy. Second, from the viewpoint of national unity, we must take into account the grievances of the Canadian west. It is important to have the tariffs removed as expeditiously as possible. For a long time the west has felt that while tariffs may have served to promote the so-called industries of Canada, they have continued long past the point of the infant in swaddling clothes. For those reasons, we are generally in support of the proposals in this bill.
I am particularly glad that our country is taking this position. When we look around in the world, we see that our neighbour to the south is moving in the opposite direction. Every indication is that the United States is going to be more restrictive in terms of its trade pattern rather than less restrictive. While Japan does not operate the tariff system as a restrictive system, the effect is as great or greater than if it had high tariffs. I wish I were as sanguine about the possibility of getting into the European Common Market as is the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). The Common Market was set up under conditions which make it very difficult for other

countries to participate. In some ways, tariffs are becoming less important than they were as an indicator of the movement of goods. There are other kinds of restriction imposed on the free passage of commodities. For example, in recent years we have seen countries contriving to keep the value of their currency unnaturally low. Today, this is of more significance than tariffs. In Japan, difficulties are obviously put in the way of imports. They are not spelled out, they are not obvious, but somehow or other nobody can meet the right person in order to reach an agreement. So, as we look round the world, despite diminished tariff restrictions there are still many obstacles in the way of the free movement of goods from one country to another.
It is popular at the moment to talk about wage and price controls as a means of reducing prices to the consumer. There is very little evidence to support the contention that this would indeed be the effect. But there is evidence to show that the consumer could be helped by the removal of some of the tariff restrictions which presently exist. This help goes beyond the mere saving of the amount of money which the government forgos by way of revenue. He is helped because goods entering Canada free of tariff produce a situation which calls for competitive action in our own marketplace and helps keep the price of goods produced in Canada at a low level. Thus, excise tax reductions would have a greater effect on prices than some of the suggestions which have been made in favour of wage and price controls.
Having said this, I will admit there are dangers facing us as we lower tariffs-dangers the government should take into account. If the government continues, as in the past, to encourage the export of raw materials, non-renewable resources, energy supplies and so on, it will be doing a terrible disservice to the nation. A reduction in tariffs could become a menace, for if we continue to export large supplies of raw materials and energy resources, and the value of our dollar rises as a consequence, the entire trade pattern of imports into Canada will be distorted. It is, therefore, of enormous importance that, in conjunction with tariff reductions, the government should ration in one way or another the export of raw materials and energy supplies. If this is not done, the value of our dollar will rise and a double threat against our industry will develop. If anything, our dollar is over-valued now, for the very reason that we have exported unfinished goods too extensively. In some ways all this has little to do with tariffs, yet it is a necessary part of state policy if we are to fight the dangers which could flow from tariff reductions. There are benefits attaching to tariff reductions, but there are also dangers.
The proposals now before us may constitute one of the most significant parts of the budget as an indicator of the way this country is going. Tax reductions and exemptions are very important, it is true, and I do not want in any to detract from their importance. But as an indicator of the direction in which Canada is going these tariff reductions are even more important. I hope we shall see continued reductions in tariffs. I also hope the government will take counter action to make sure that the value of our dollar does not rise too high as a result of our exporting unfinished goods.
April 13, 1973

Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to the minister's statement on Bill C-172 announcing a reduction in customs tariff that will apply to developing countries.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party, I say that we are fully support this bill precisely because while protecting the interests of the producers it will certainly meet the wishes of the consumers in that we have found three ways of helping less fortunate countries.
We can help them by granting them interest-free loans. We do this fairly regularly every year. When those loans are granted through new credits from the Bank of Canada we are very happy because they do not affect the worker, industry, or the consumer; they are merely new credits intended to help developing countries.
Secondly, we help them by granting them interest-free loans on money taken out of the budget of Canada. In that case, Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of greater concern to Canadians, because it would mean lending their tax money without interest to developed countries. It is to a good end, but the means are rather coude when you consider what has happened in the last few years. On one occasion, for example, we realized that we did not have enough money to lend to a certain underdeveloped country-which I will not name here, but all hon. members will recognize it. And so we had to borrow $25 million at 8 per cent, to lend to the underdeveloped country without interest for 60 years. That is really smart, Mr. Speaker! But is has happened here, in Parliament: we borrow money abroad for no-interest loans to countries we want to help.
I am very pleased about the hon. minister's announcement this afternoon, because I think that the best way to help the underdeveloped countries is not just to reduce our customs tariffs by two thirds, but to abolish them altogether, so that these countries can trade with ours, to the benefit of the whole of Canada, and especially to that of the consumer.
It is well known that some customs duties double the price of food products coming from those countries. If the consumer could buy imported products at half price, I think he would be very happy about it. When the committee on trends in food prices carried out its study, we observed that high customs barriers were one of the major causes of the high prices of imported foods. They sometimes increase food prices by 20, 25 or 30 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, this is a fine opportunity for the minister to abolish them completely, on a trial basis.
The minister says that we can trade with 77 countries. It would be possible to eliminate all customs duties; the minister has announced that they would be reduced by two thirds. I argue that these countries could be exempted from all customs duties on food, fruit, and meat. I shall say a few words about it later on.
I suggest that these would mean a healthy competition for our Canadian producers without doing them any harm. Of course this will not come about. If the consumer does not want any competition on the pretent that we are going to protect our industries and Canadian producers, what
Customs Tariff
will happen to a product unable to be fairly competitive? It is allowed to enter our country, but its price will be doubled or tripled in order to protect producers. But who is paying, Mr. Speaker? It is always the consumer. We are going to protect 100, 125 or 200 people at the expense of 20 million Canadians. It is to this point that I wish to draw the minister's attention and even encourage him to entirely eliminate customs duties in our relations with these countries.
As far as the protection of our industries is concerned, I believe that the list which is proposed here, especially as regards agricultural products, is very reasonable. There may be a few farmers will wonder about. I am referring to canned meat. I cannot say for sure, but I think that most of these products, according to a serious analysis, are not competing with similar Canadian products.
Once more, if the minister allows these products to enter our country, as I said earlier, this will serve the consumers' interests. A little earlier, I heard the previous speaker deal with the British preferential tariff. I do not know to what extent England benefits from the preferential tariff, but as far as I know, England is not an underdeveloped country.
That is why I am trying to find out what countries are involved. There was a mention of Spain, Portugal and so on. The main analysis will be made at this stage and I fail to understand, like the previous speaker, that it is normal to forever extend the preferential tariff to England and never to France.
If it is normal, it is a quite irregular normal thing.
Once again, I do not wish to discuss this further. I only wish to beg the minister to push a little further ahead and not to fear to deal with developping countries. This would be a good occasion for Canada to do something for them and to sell our products. Besides, this will prevent Canada from granting them interest-free loans for a 60-year period, when we have to pay 8 per cent interest on the money used for interest-free loans to them.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to rise in support of the measures that are before us, particularly since these changes in our customs tariff will assist parts of the world that are greatly in need, not simply of material aid but of this kind of help. We have moved to a time in our relationship with the developing countries when we should give priority to trade rather than aid, as understood in the sense that was appropriate a generation ago.
The move the government is making through the proposals in this bill is one that I think will receive support from both sides of the House as well as throughout the country. We are part of one world and we want to express this fact in our economic policies as in other things, particularly at this time when we think of the call of some of our spiritual communions and leaders throughout the country for ten days of development. This is a political measure which I think can be taken as a positive response to that summons. One of the best ways we can help developing countries in the world is by giving those countries the opportunity to trade with those who can be their customers.

April 13, 1973
Customs Tariff
But we have to think about another side of the coin as well, and that is the way in which the administration of our customs and tariff policies bear upon Canadian business and Canadian working people. This afternoon I want to focus the attention of the House precisely, though briefly, upon one aspect of this, namely the way in which our so-called duty free stores along the border of Canada are administered. I believe they are administered in ways which are injurious to Canadian business and particularly to the gift industry.
We have several of these duty free stores in Canada, chiefly at international airports though also at two seaports. The way in which these stores are administered prevents the sale of many manufactures, particularly the products of the gift industry. Representations have been made by members of that industry to the government over the year, and at times members of the industry have been persuaded that they were being listened to by the government-I think better listened to than this debate is being listened to by the government. Companies participating in the gift industry have still not seen any positive action or remedies taken by the government. Therefore, I am disappointed that the proposals of the government for tariff and excise reform will not, as far as I can see, make any provision for solving the problem to which I have referred. If we were to open up our duty free stores to Canadian manufacturers, particularly to products of our gift industry, we would be increasing the possibility of their development and increasing job opportunities in Canada, because one of the most labour intensified parts of our economy is the tourist industry. With the gift industry dove-tailing into that, the House can readily see how this could be beneficial in helping to solve our unemployment problems.
I would very earnestly suggest that the government listen with renewed seriousness to the appeal of the gift industry throughout Canada that steps be taken to open up our duty-free shops so more Canadian manufacturers can avail themselves of them. I hope as well that they can be opened at more of our border crossing points; that is the kind of duty-free store to which I have referred. At the present time they are located almost exclusively at international airports, yet there is a tremendous amount of tourist traffic across the border by car, by bus and by railroad.
I think the government would be doing more to help Canadian business, the Canadian economy and working people if it took a positive step in this direction. This is not in contradiction to the kind of ideal to which I referred in my opening remarks, also referred to by the minister. The more we can do to stimulate Canadian business, the more we can do to help strengthen our own economy, the better position we are in to reach out a helping hand to other parts of the world.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. McCleave in the chair.

speakeroldname: Mr. J.-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for having given me the responsibility of piloting this bill in the House and I wish to assure him that I will do my best to have it passed in the shortest possible time. Mr. Speaker, bills on financing and guarantee were tabled every year with the exception of the 1963 bill which applied to 1962-63 and that of 1966 which applied to 1965-66 as well as this one which applies to 1972-73. Hon. members will remember that the 1971 bill-which included certain provisions for 1971 and 1972-had not been read for the second time when the twenty-eighth Parliament was dissolved. This bill brings back those provisions.
This bill for 1973 is basically the same as those for previous years. It sets out in a concised form the capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railway Company for 1973 as outlined in its capital budget for that year which amounts to $225,500,000. This bill also authorizes the company to make expenditures not exceeding $75 million between January 1 and July 1, 1974 for the purpose of discharging obligations incurred prior to January 1, 1974, and to enter into contracts prior to July 1, 1974 for capital expenditures not exceeding $167,500,000 that become due and payable after 1973. These expenditures and commitments are according to the investment budget of the company for 1973.
The bill aims at fulfilling six major objectives most of whom have already been similarly outlined in the previous bills on financing and guaranteed.
First, the bill includes provisions allowing the Canadian National Railways Company to borrow up to $21 million to finance the construction of sidings. This amount includes the financing of sidings more than 20 miles long whose construction is authorized by a special act, as well as the financing of tracks less than 20 miles long whose construction does not require any authority under a special act. By including all sidings, this provision reflects the intention of taking into account, in the bill on the financing and guarantee, all the funds that the Canadian National Railways Company may require.
Second, the bill provides for the Department of Finance to continue purchasing Canadian National preferred shares bearing interest at 4 per cent during 1972 and until the end of calendar year 1973. This provision perpetuates the practice established by former financing and guarantee, legislation. The 1970 act postponed to December 31, 1971 the expiry date of the authorization granted by the 1952 Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act for the purchase of such shares to the extent of 3 per cent of the company's gross income.
Third, as in former years, the bill authorizes the government to extend temporary advances to Canadian National and Air Canada in order to meet operating income deficit for the period of January 1, 1973 to June 30, 1974. These advances will be reimbursed later on in the year from company income. Should such income prove insufficient,
CNR and Air Canada
the outstanding balance will be met through deficit appropriation by parliament.

In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call your attention to a proposal for a change in the policy relative to appointment of auditors.
Since auditing the books of the CNR and Air Canada represents considerable work, the government came to the conclusion that this work should not be entrusted to a single firm of auditors, to the exclusion of all others. The government considers rather that this job should be periodically assigned on a rotation basis to large Canadian auditing firms. Thus new method and approaches would come to bear on the operation of these two companies which, according to the government, would be beneficial for all concerned.
If the policy of rotating auditors were adopted, we should have to study carefully the frequency of the rotation. Evidently, the duration of the assignment should not be too short, because, otherwise, the auditors would hardly have enough time to familiarize themselves with the operations of the company and the intricacies of its accounting system, not to mention the special accounting requirements of the Canadian Transport Commission.
On the other hand, the long-term appointments made in the past covered far too long periods. Consequently, it was agreed that a five to six years' appointment would be an acceptable compromise, the first year and the last year to be overlapping periods during which two auditing firms would be hired. That way, during the overlapping period, the incoming auditor for a new term could progressively take over the work of the outgoing auditor, ensuring the necessary continuity of auditing. Section 14 of the bill deals with that situation.

April 13, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
In conclusion, I should like to add that the government intends, every five or six years, to recommend to parliament rotation of the independent auditors.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again parliament is faced with a bill which purports to ask parliamentary approval for moneys used in financing Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. Before I come to my main remarks I should like to refer briefly to some of the comments the parliamentary secretary just made. He started by asking that parliament adopt this bill as quickly as possible. When we dig into the bill and the circumstances behind it, I can well understand why the government would like to have it passed as quickly as possible and thereby put an embarrassing piece of legislation where it perhaps belongs, under the rug. I say to the minister there is no real urgency to pass this bill. There was no urgency last year to pass it; the government in effect ignored it. This bill provides for expenditures to the end of June, 1974. Therefore, I for one will not be beguiled by the government's plea of great urgency in respect of passage of this bill.
The government has many questions to answer before we on this side of the House would agree to grant it the amount of money involved in a bill such as this. I have not totalled the amounts but I believe they run close to $1 billion. I know $1 billion does not mean much to the government, but in talking of an amount of money of this size I feel it is incumbent on the opposition to examine very closely what kind of monkeyshine has been going on here.
The parliamentary secretary said this bill takes up where the last one left off. We know better than that. It does not take up where the last one left off. The last bill of this kind which passed through this House was the 1970 financing bill. That is the only piece of legislation we have had. Certainly this bill does not take up where that one left off. As a matter of fact, it does not even take up where the aborted Bill C-4 left off, because there is a six months' lapse there which is not included in this bill.
When I first looked at Bill C-164, my immediate reaction was that it was the usual financing bill with the same old wording, and there were no changes except perhaps slight ones in respect of the amounts required. I read the bill through and could not find too many changes until I went back to the preamble. Suddenly the meat of the whole thing struck me. It is in the preamble, which say that Bill C-164 is-
An act to authorize the provision of moneys... for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973, to the 30th day of June, 1974-
My first reaction on reading those words was that obviously there was a misprint, that it must be intended to be from the 1st day of January, 1971. However, I checked the bill throughout and found that in every place where there was any reference to dates, the same dates appeared. Obviously, the government's drafters are not so stupid as to have made such drafting errors; therefore, the government is asking us now to approve appropriations for the CNR when for the last two years, we have not approved any.
[Mr. Comtois.l
In my remarks last year on Bill C-4 I described the debate on that bill as an exercise in futility. Had I known then what was going to happen, I would have used much stronger language. This is much more than an exercise in futility. It is a downright, deliberate degradation of the rights of parliament to bring in such a bill.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
