speechtext:
I think the government wants to forget about Bill C-4, but I do not believe we can discuss Bill C-164 properly unless we discuss it in the context of Bill C-4. Bill C-4 was never enacted. It was introduced in the last session of the last parliament. It was entitled "Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee Act, 1971". It is rather interesting that the parliamentary secretary made only a casual, fleeting reference to Bill C-4, but he dealt at length with the financing bill of 1970. He probably did that because the financing bill of 1970 was the last bill to give this government any right to appropriate moneys.
Ever since parliament passed that bill, the government has either been breaking the law or circumventing it in such a way as to destroy the rights of parliament to control the spending of money. Whether this was a deliberate attempt to have the cabinet gradually take over all control of spending, or whether it was just a continuation of the slipshod handling of legislation which we saw in the last parliament, is not for me to judge. But the fact remains that this government is continuing the practice which was developed in the last parliament and continued now in many areas. It is an attempt to take away the control of money bills from parliament, where such control rightly belong, and give it to the government and treasury board.
This bill is a crude attempt to fool us into believing that the control of the purse-strings still rests with us. It is a crude attempt to hide the fact that this government is deliberately eroding the right of parliament to control moneys. It is a desperate attempt to camouflage what has been going on ever since this government came into office. There are many examples of this type of action that I could refer to, but I will not go into them now. They have been the subject of debate in this House. My colleague, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has mentioned some of them.
I should like to refer briefly to glaring examples of the type of procedure this government is following. One, of course, is the famous Polymer fiasco where the government asked parliament to give approval to action which they had taken without even letting parliament see the annual report or the audited statements of the company in question. It was interesting to hear the minister state at the time that since Polymer was losing money, the government would bail it out. But it was much more interesting shortly thereafter, when the audited statements of Polymer came out, to see that instead of losing money the company was showing an increase in profit.
The second glaring example was the horrible fiasco created in the Unemployment Insurance Commission's accounts. We all know what happened there and I will not dwell on it. I have spoken on it before. Here, again, is a deliberate attempt by the government to do by subterfuge
April 13, 1973

what they could not do by law. This bill wants us to approve expenditures past and future for two Crown corporations, and in neither case do we have either an audited statement or an annual report.
Some hon. members are businessmen and a good many of them are lawyers. I ask them a simple question: What would happen if they, as directors of or legal advisers to corporations, were faced with a request from the board of directors to appropriate, say, $1 million dollars and they were not given an annual report as to what had happened the year before, or an audited statement? This government asks us to do something we certainly would not do in our own businesses. We are being asked now to approve a large amount of money for these two corporations, but we have neither their annual report nor their audited statements. We do not know what has been done with the money that was granted previously.
After I read the preamble to this bill I wondered what had happened in the two previous years. If these companies need the money to operate-and we know the government always had to bail both of them out so they could at least meet their loan payments-where did they get the money with which to operate? As I remember, in other years we were told the same as we were told today, that there was a great deal of urgency and that if we did not pass the bill the CNR would not be able to meet their payroll, would not be able to buy new equipment, and Air Canada would not be able to buy new aircraft. We were told we had to pass the bill otherwise the wheels of these two great corporations would stop turning.
Therefore I began to investigate where these two corporations got the money to keep them going in 1971 and 1972. This is why I went back to Bill C-4 and reviewed what had happened. Bill C-4 covered the financing period from January 1, 1971, to June 30, 1972. The summary of events is very interesting in light of recent statements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others on the government side that the opposition has been holding up the business of the House. Here is a classic example of a government with an absolute majority which nevertheless refused to bring in legislation, for what reason we do not know. They refused to allow the legislation to proceed through to passage. When you read the history, it seems there was something about which the government were so embarrassed that they did not dare bring the bill back.
The bill received first reading on February 21, 1972. It came back for second reading on March 6, 1972. On April 21 the debate on second reading was adjourned. The government never again brought the bill before parliament during the life of the last parliament. The annual report and audited statements of the CNR were not tabled by the then minister of transport until May 11. This may be just a coincidence, but it was after the government had cut off proceedings on April 21.
The Air Canada report and audit were tabled only on April 17, four days before the bill died effectively on the order paper. On June 21 the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), as reported at page 3348 of Hansard, asked the then minister of transport to have the government refer these two reports of CN and Air Canada to the
CNR and Air Canada
Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. The minister replied that such action was for the government House leader to determine, but that he had no objection. The government never made any reference to the committee. This was a bill, we were told at that time-just as we are told today about Bill C-164-that was a matter of some urgency, and we would have to get the bill through the House or these two Crown agencies could not operate because their funds would dry up. But that bill died at the end of that session.
In this session, Bill C-164 was introduced on March 19 of this year. This bill, as the parliamentary secretary has outlined, relates to the financing period from January 1, 1973, to June 30, 1974.1 emphasize those dates because they carry a great deal of significance. The only retroactive provision with respect to the year 1972 appears to be in clause 13, but this is not clarified in the explanatory note. I will deal with clause 13 a little later in my remarks, but I would point out to the House now that it has to do with the appointment of auditors. I have been involved in business a little, Mr. Speaker, and never have I heard a board of directors ask for the appointment of auditors after the year has elapsed. The normal thing is to appoint auditors before the year begins. Here we are being asked to appoint them retroactively to January 1, 1972.
With all this time lapse, we have had no bill on CNR financing since the 1970 bill was passed; and the government has not yet tabled the annual report and audit of the CN for 1972. This is why I want to refer to clause 13. Maybe there is a reason for that. Who were the auditors? By what authority did they act? Maybe this is why we cannot get the CN annual report. The annual report and audit of the CN have not been tabled here, but the government did table the CN operating and capital budgets for the calendar year 1972. However, this was done only on February 28, 1973, although the government had approved these budgets on August 28, 1972, by order in council P.C. 1972/1865.
What is the situation with respect to the present bill? We have a period covering CNR and Air Canada financing from January 1, 1971, to June 30, 1974-three and a half years-with a six months' hiatus that extends from July 1, 1972, to December 31, 1972, that was covered in the previous bill. I am not saying that is included in this bill; I am saying that in that three and a half years period there is six months from January 1, 1971, to June 30, 1972, in which apparently nothing happened. It was included in the previous bill, but then there is another six-month period from July, 1972, to December, 1972, that does not appear anywhere. It was not in the old bill and it is not in this bill.
Where did the CN and Air Canada get their money during that six-month period? Personally, I am not going to heed the parliamentary secretary's appeal to rush this bill through the House, because I want answers to these questions. Again the House is asked to consider Bill C-164 with a gun held to its head by the government because approval of this bill is approval, in part, of capital and operating expenditures of public funds which have already been spent or committed without approval of parliament.
If it was not obvious before, it is now clear beyond doubt that the annual CNR financing bill is an exercise in

April 13, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
futility, a waste of time and an affront to the House. It is also obvious that the financial affairs of the CNR and Air Canada are controlled by the government, and by the government alone. The annual financing bill is simply a mockery to delude the public and its representatives in this House that they control the public's two greatest and most vital public utilities. Anybody who has sat on committees and spoken to officials of Air Canada and CNR has sensed the feeling of smug superiority and contempt that they hold for parliament because they know we have no power.
It does not matter how much we cry or beg, the decisions, legal or otherwise, are made by the government. This is what is taking place. Presumably the key to the government's financial control is contained in section 30 of the Canadian National Railways Act, chapter C-10 of the 1970 Revised Statutes, and the Air Canada Act, chapter A-ll of the 1970 Revised Statutes. Section 30 of the CNR act provides:
the National company may also borrow upon its notes or securities or the notes or securities of any such other company-
That is, any other company comprised in the CNR system.
-whether for its own benefit or for the benefit of such other company or otherwise.
In section 13(3) of the Air Canada Act there is provision that the CNR may lend money to Air Canada. There was something interesting about this that I suddenly discovered on reading the auditor's report to parliament for the year ended December 31, 1971. It was an item under the heading "Long-term Debt." On January 1, 1972, a $100 million debenture matured and a promissory note in the same amount was issued to the Minister of Finance to pay for it. When I read that I started to wonder what kind of financing was taking place. It seemed the CNR needed $100 million to retire these debentures held by the government so it said to the government, "We will give you a promissory note for $100 million." We have no way of knowing about this until we see the annual report and audited statements of the CNR.
In essence, the CNR has only to give the government a promissory note for whatever hundred of millions of dollars of taxpayers' money that it wants; and if Air Canada wants money also, it can include that sum in the amount on the face of the promissory note. The result is that the government gains control over the operations of CNR and Air Canada. The real board of directors of both corporations then becomes the cabinet. And, of course, that cabinet control is immeasurably strengthened when the president of the Canadian Transport Commission is invariably a former member of the government. It goes right down the line and you cannot get away from it. But what does the CNR act say about budgets? Section 37(1) reads as follows:
The annual budget of National Railways shall be under the control of the board of directors and shall be submitted by the board of directors to the Minister of Transport.
(2)	The Minister of Transport shall annually lay before parliament the budget of National Railways approved by the governor in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance.
(3)	The annual budget of National Railways shall include estimates of the amounts required

(a)	for income deficits,
(b)	for capital expenditures,
(c)	for refunding or retirement of maturing securities, and
(d)	for additional working capital.
I suppose the government can say that it fulfilled this provision, that it laid the budget on the table of this House. But there it died. Parliament had nothing to do about either refusing or giving consent to these expenditures of moneys which amount to some $1 billion every year.
Considering these facts, one cannot help wondering at the realistic cynicism of the government in deliberately letting the CNR financing bill die on the order paper in the last parliament, in withholding the annual report while the second reading debate was going on in this House, in refusing to refer the reports of CNR and Air Canada to the appropriate committee of this House, and in perpetuating this empty farce of presenting a bill before the House for second reading while withholding from the House the 1972 annual report and audited statements of both corporations.
What does the Railway Act say about the annual report? Section 39(1) of the Railway Act provides:
The board of directors shall make a report annually to parliament setting forth the results of their operations-
And so on. It goes on to say what they shall do. They are to set forth-
-the results of their operations, the amounts expended on capital account in respect of National Railways and such other information as appears to them to be of public interest or necessary for the information of parliament with relation to any situation existing at the time of such report.
No matter how you read that section, there is a definite commitment on cabinet and on the board of directors of the company to submit these reports to parliament for approval. This the government has refused to do. That shows contempt for parliament and contempt for the people of Canada. The government has made only one mistake-perhaps I wrong the government; perhaps it is not a mistake-it has shown contempt for the laws of Canada as enacted by parliament. Section 38(1) of the act provides:
A continuous audit of the accounts of National Railways shall be made by independent auditors appointed annually by Parliament who shall annually report to parliament in respect of their audit.
The same provision is made in section 12 of the Air Canada Act with respect to Air Canada. It provides:
The accounts and financial transactions of the corporation shall be audited by the auditor appointed by parliament-
Then come these significant words:
-to audit the accounts of the Canadian National Railways.
The law. as written by parliament, stipulates that the CNR auditors and, necessarily, those of Air Canada must be appointed each year by parliament. Let us go back to clause 13.

The law, as written by parliament, spells out that a firm of auditors must be appointed each year by parliament. The government paid no heed to that; they did not lay the legislation before us in that regard. Their refusal so to do shows their arrogance, their contempt for this House and for the people of Canada. Further, they show contempt for the board of directors of Air Canada and the board of directors of Canadian National Railways. The government asks us to pass the bill before us as quickly as possible; I am beginning to understand why it wants it passed without discussion.
In clause 14(2) of the present bill we find this language:
For the purpose of carrying out the audit described in subsection (1), the following firms of chartered acccounts are appointed as independent auditors:
Get this, Mr. Speaker:
(a) for the year 1972, the firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co., of the cities of Toronto and Montreal-
I ask, what kind of business practice do we see here, in which directors go to the shareholders and ask them to appoint auditors retroactively? What continuing records are to be used? Where are the auditors to start? Where are they to find the necessary records? As I say, how are they to make an audit? Is that why there is no CNR Annual report and no audited statement? That is what I have asked myself, and I have not found the answer. I hope answers will be forthcoming, for the government's sake. It compounds the confusion and the crime by saying, "Oh, but we have discovered an answer. We will tell parliament that the system of appointing the same auditors year after year is not a good one; we have to spread the business around a little." I am not implying why it would want to spread the business around; I do not know.

Here we have one firm appointed for 1972. That firm, with another firm, has been appointed for 1973. From the way this government has been extorting revenue from the taxpayer, I suppose it can afford to hire three or four firms, although I do not think that we as members of the House should authorize it.
I think I have made the point I have been trying to make. Normally, in debates such as this people talk about the debts of the CNR. It seems that the debts of Air Canada are almost in the same category as those of the CNR because many of the things you can say about the operation of the CNR can be applied to the operation of Air Canada. If I had time to make further remarks I would make it clear that I am not as critical of the CNR and Air Canada as I am of the government which refuses to enunciate and formulate a national transportation policy year after year. I raised this subject last year with the president of Air Canada and he complained bitterly that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) would not tell him on what basis the airline should be operated, whether in the public interest or for profit. I was interested to read a report in the Financial Post to the effect that Mr. Pratt, who I believe was chairman of the board, was waiting for the minister to take action, and now he is at the point of throwing up his hands and taking off for sunnier climes.
I have said some of the things I wanted to say. I know that my colleagues will not neglect the CNR in this debate; neither will they ignore Air Canada, the company which is rapidly taking over the position of CNR and which may be instrumental in getting CNR off the hook. Air Canada seems to be doing its best to downgrade service in the field of passenger accommodation, in service in the air and on the ground, and is reducing flights to the minimum permissible. It is doing its best to get the CNR off the hook. I believe that my colleagues and others who will follow me in the debate will express somewhat less than satisfaction with the operations of CN and Air Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I participate in this debate because of the significance of this financing bill in terms of the operations of Canadian National Railways and Air Canada, the spending in terms of the overall effect of transportation in this country, how it affects many regions, particularly the west and the Maritimes and how important transportation is to the development of a strong Canadian nation.
The hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) raised a number of questions of great interest. They can be summed up by asking the parliamentary secretary, or possibly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), one simple question: How did CNR and Air Canada do their financing in 1971 and 1972? That seems to sum up the remarks of the hon. member for Moncton which I believe to be appropriate.
When this bill comes before parliament it gives members an opportunity to review the question of transportation as it affects this country from one end to the other. I hope that members of the government will espouse and outline some aspects of the policy that is needed in the area of national transportation. Further to this, so many ministers of the Crown have their fingers in the pie of transportation that if we were to try to load them all on a streetcar, we would have to hire an additional one to carry them.
I hope the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board will outline how the Canada Grains Council is operating and who is financing it. I hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) will outline his area of jurisdiction and tell us what changes we can expect in the area of freight rates and in developing a co-ordinated transportation policy. Also, I hope he will outline the policy related to the development of harbours at the port of Churchill and other places.
The Minister of Finance, who moves this bill every year, ought to outline some of the changes in financing the CNR and Air Canada, and with regard to the CNR debt which occurred as a result of buying-out the Mackenzie and Mann railway, thus getting a private interest out of hock, in the early twenties. The Canadian people have been paying for it ever since.
I hope that within the confines of this debate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) will reflect upon the pension situation of retired railroaders and the question of collective agreements which date back to 1956. Perhaps he has an opinion on this matter and will use his good offices to try to bring about an improvement in the situation of retired railroad pensioners.
Debate on the financing of CNR and Air Canada is an annual event. During these debates there is considerable

objection raised to certain aspects of the national transportation policy or the fact that one does not seem to exist. The Minister of Transport was formerly in charge of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I am sure he is well aware of the problems of developing those regions in this country which are at an economic disadvantage in relation to the golden horseshoe of Ontario. As he was formerly in charge of DREE, he should be aware of the effect of freight rates in terms of the kind of growth that is needed in the west, in the Maritimes and in northern Ontario.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) sat for several years as minister of transport. He ought to be aware of the effect of freight rates and transportation upon regional development. These two ministers should be able to co-ordinate a program to alleviate the difficulties in terms of developing a program to end regional disparity. With their vast experience, they should be able to come up with a policy that has some teeth in it to develop the various regions of this country on a basis equal to the golden horseshoe of Ontario.
I wish to deal with a number of points which are significant to this bill. As stated previously by my colleagues, the whole question of allocating certain moneys in relation to the CNR debt, which relates back to the time the Mackenzie and Mann railroad was purchased to get Liberal promoters and developers off the hook, needs revision. There was some change in the relationship of the debt several years ago. There is further need to take this debt off the back of Canadian National Railways. I hope the government will give consideration to this question within the realm of this bill.
Some things are very aggravating to those of us who come from western Canada, northern Ontario and the Maritimes. I refer to the national transportation policy and the disgusting inequity in the freight rates structure. There is no greater burden on western development than the freight rates structure which was initially set up to protect the developing manufacturing industries in southern Ontario. That freight rates structure has been with us ever since. We have lived with the burden of freight rates at the same time as we have lived with the burden of tariffs.
In the Speech from the Throne the government outlined its concern for meeting the discrimination against western Canada in the area of transportation. They have set up a western premiers' conference for July to deal with western economic problems. One fundamental question they must tackle is that of freight rates. I wish to quote some figures to indicate how freight rates affect western Canada. I first wish to deal with commodities purchased from the east. On goods shipped from Contrecoeur, Quebec, to Vancouver, the revenue for the railroads is $1.02 per ton-mile. If the same commodity is shipped to Regina, the revenue per ton-mile is $2.55. On goods shipped from Quebec to Saskatoon, the revenue per ton-mile is $2.59.
Looking at the other side, the rail revenue per ton-mile for eastern steel products terminating at Vancouver is $1.02. The rail revenue per ton-mile to Regina is $2.55. There is a 150 per cent increase in revenue for goods moving to Regina compared with those being moved to
April 13, 1973

Vancouver. In relation to Saskatoon, the increase amounts to 154 per cent. At this point I would refer to an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of April 11 on the question of western freight rates. This is a further example of the discrimination we face. It reads:
Rapeseed, which is grown in Alberta, can be shipped raw from Lethbridge to Montreal for 81 cents per 100 lbs; but if it is processed into oil and meal it cost $1.22 per hundred pounds to ship the product to Montreal. Alberta would like to know if there is a cost relationship between the differing rates for the raw and processed product-which it suspects there isn't-or if the railways are setting industrial policy through their rates. The railways refuse to give any cost-relationship information. All this has so annoyed Alberta that it has produced its own transportation policy, covering air-international as well as domestic-highway and rail.
Similar moves have taken place in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. If we are really concerned about national unity, certain important elements in our economic make-up must be fundamentally changed. One of these is freight rates. In the constituency of Assiniboia, with which I am most familiar, we ship our basic commodity, wheat, by rail. Branch lines were built to provide this service. Out of all the rail lines in the constituency, 605 miles of track are scheduled for abandonment by the CN or by the CP. Situated along those lines is elevator capacity sufficient to hold 11.5 million bushels of grain. These elevators are to be closed down. In past years, an average of 22.5 million bushels of grain has been carried over those tracks. In future, this grain would have to be moved by truck. More than 5,100 producers in the constituency would be affected by the removal of these tracks. Every dirt road and municipal road would be affected. Tax losses to municipalities would amount to between 50 and 60 per cent of their total revenue.
The bill before us offers an opportunity to deal with the question of national transportation policy. If the government allows the wholesale abandonment of rail lines in western Canada, it will be carrying an enormous burden of responsibility. I draw attention to the fact that producers living near those lines have been offered no concrete alternative means of moving their grain. We are hopeful that in the course of this debate the minister will be able to give us an undertaking that the final decision to abandon these lines will be deferred beyond the 1975 date originally determined. Certainly, there is the odd branch line which may have to be shut down. I wish hon. members could see a map of my constituency. If these lines are shut down, there will be hardly any left; it will create a gap some 50 miles by 75 miles in extent in the middle of the riding. This is where the greatest burden will fall if services are discontinued in a wholesale manner.
I see I have only about one minute left, and there are a number of questions which I intend to address to the minister and which, I trust, will be answered. If I might be allowed to call it four o'clock, I shall continue next week.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. C. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE THAT REPRESENTATIVE OF MUNICIPALITIES SERVE ON NANAIMO HARBOUR COMMISSION
speechtext:
that Bill C-21, to amend the Harbour Commissions Act (Nanaimo Harbour Commission) be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move that Bill C-21 be given second reading and sent to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, I have two purposes in mind. The first is to provide for local representation on the Nanaimo Harbour Commission. Section 4(1) of the Harbour Commissions Act provides that a harbour commission shall consist of not less than three and not more than five members. Section 5(1) provides that there shall be one representative from the local municipality and, if there is more than one local municipality, that a second representative shall be on the commission.
In the case of the Nanaimo Harbour Commission there are only three commissioners, two appointed by the gover-

April 13, 1973
Harbour Commissions Act
nor in council and one by the city of Nanaimo. The two representatives appointed by the governor in council are the chairman and a second member who is also the solicitor for the commission. But there is no representative from the adjoining municipalities, despite the fact that the act provides for this.
The provision of the bill which I am now asking the House to approve and to send to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications asks that it be made mandatory to have five members on the Nanaimo Harbour Commission, three of whom would be appointed by the governor in council, one to be appointed by the city of Nanaimo and one by the regional district board.
Some hon. members may ask, why this insistence upon local representation on the harbour commission? I suggest that there can be no intelligent planning of harbour facilities unless the local authorities have an effective voice in determining the course to be followed, the location of streets and access roads, the effect upon the shoreline of any expansion of the harbour facilities, and in the matter of traffic control. All of these are of direct concern to the local authorities. Therefore, unless the harbour commission works in conjunction with the elected representatives of the local council, the result will be chaos.
There has been an example of this kind of lack of consultation and co-ordination in the Nanaimo harbour commission's operations recently. In March of last year the Nanaimo harbour commission made public a program costing some $10 million for a large extension of the harbour facilities. After this program had been announced, the city of Nanaimo's advisory planning commission looked into the matter and registered their objection to the location. The regional district board also looked into this matter and expressed their dissatisfaction with the location. Groups of interested citizens, for a variety of reasons, also expressed their opposition to the location that had been selected and some of the Indians of No. 1 Indian reserve were quite upset about the proposals.
In addition to that, the Department of the Environment expressed some concern. Some of the departmental officials stated in correspondence which I have that they had not been consulted. I have no way of knowing whether or not that is true, but the department and certain conservation groups were disturbed about the fact that the extension of the harbour facilities was going to block off part of the estuary of the Nanaimo River. The department was also concerned about dredging and backfilling and the effect this would have on marine and wildlife in the area.
The result was that .the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) managed to get a stay of proceedings and appointed a task force to look into this matter. I am not familiar with the report of the task force, but I do know that as a result of its report the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) referred the whole matter to the Canada Ports and Harbours Planning Committee. I commend the minister for agreeing to have this committee hold public hearings in the city of Nanaimo on January 25, at which time various groups expressed their opinions. I think it is safe to say, having looked over the briefs, that the majority of them thought this matter should be investigated further.
I have a press release dated April 10 in which the Minister of Transport said that as a result of the report of

the planning committee he has decided to accept their recommendation for an in-depth study of this harbour development. It is expected that this study, which will be conducted by specialists from the Department of Transport, the Department of the Environment, the Department of Urban Affairs and the Department of Public Works, will report before the end of this year.
I cite these facts, Mr. Speaker, in order to point out that lack of co-ordination and consultation prior to a project being launched can cause a great deal of difficulty in a community. It seems to me that there is need for making mandatory provision that there be adequate representation on the Nanaimo Harbour Commission-and I think this ought to apply to all commissions-from local governing bodies. This is why I have introduced Bill C-21.
My second reason for introducing this bill is that I hope the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications will give some thought to making recommendations to the Minister of Transport regarding a complete revision of the Harbour Commissions Act. In the years that I have been in this House, I have noted that members with ports in their constituencies have repeatedly expressed dissatisfaction with the Harbour Commissions Act as being archaic and undemocratic. Successive ministers of transport have said that new legislation was being considered, but so far nothing has been done to correct a situation that in my opinion is becoming intolerable.
I have a press release dated March 27, issued by the Minister of Transport, in which he says that the National Ports Council has been asked to make recommendations regarding a revision of the Harbour Commissions Act. That is perfectly proper. These men have the expertise to deal with the technical and engineering aspects of the ports. But engineering is only part of the problem; the people of the community and those planning the affairs of the community are equally important.
I hope the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications will take a look at the whole act to see whether or not there is provision in it for co-ordinated effort between the different departments of government, local authorities and harbour commissions.
I am not finding fault with any particular harbour commission or with any particular group of men. What I am saying is that there is a deficiency in the act itself in that there is failure to provide the machinery for adequate consultation and co-ordination.
The establishment of port authorities has grown up like Topsy-small bodies of men clothed with immense power and responsibility, controlled only by the Minister of Transport. These commissions have the power to buy, sell or lease property. They have power to expropriate land and borrow money, only subject to the approval of the Minister of Transport. Each harbour commission proceeds in its own way. Some do better than others, but they have autocratic powers which are at variance with the whole principle of participatory democracy.
The Harbour Commissions Act sets up little autocracies with wide powers subject only to the government granting them funds for capital expansion and guidelines set forth by the Minister of Transport through regulations. Other-
April 13, 1973

wise they can proceed to carry out developments which may be good or bad, which may coincide with local planning authorities or conflict with them. I submit that no other group has such sweeping powers.
There is no provision for co-ordination with other departments of government. The government has very wisely, but belatedly, set up the Canada Ports and Harbours Planning Committee, but this only provides for an input by federal departments and their agencies. It does nothing to ensure joint planning and consultation with local authorities.
I suggest that not only local authorities but local people have a right to be consulted if the harbour commission is proposing extensive projects which could have far reaching effects upon the community. The right to know and be heard is fundamental to democratic government. This act ought to provide for public hearings so that citizens' groups will be able to place their views before the harbour commission, not after the plans are completed and the project is begun but in the planning stage and before final decisions have been made.
At the present time the harbour commissions, provincial governments and local governing bodies are all making plans concerning the same people and the same areas; there is no provision in the legislation to provide joint planning and full consultation between the three levels of government. The Minister of Transport cannot be expected to supervise all these harbour commissions adequately. His department receives their applications for capital funds to extend harbour facilities, and if his officials are satisfied as to the need for expansion and the engineering feasibility of the project, it is approved-without any meaningful input by the people most vitally affected, namely, the people who live in the immediate vicinity of the port.
I submit, Sir, that the day is past when the public will stand for this kind of arbitrary administration of their affairs. From the government's own standpoint it should welcome the participation and co-operation of the local governing bodies and interested citizens' groups. By requiring full disclosure of information and by permitting an input from the people most concerned, the government will get better plans and more co-ordinated projects. At the same time, this will make for finer communities and more satisfied citizens.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask the House to pass this motion and give second reading to Bill C-21, in the hope that it will provide for local representation on the Nanaimo Harbour Commission. I would urge that as an ancillary benefit the committee give some thought to making recommendations to the minister for a general review of the Harbour Commissions Act so that the legislation will help to promote better co-ordination, better consultation and a more democratic way of carrying on the business of operating harbours in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE THAT REPRESENTATIVE OF MUNICIPALITIES SERVE ON NANAIMO HARBOUR COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate rather belatedly, but I am delighted to support the proposals in this measure put forward by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), my neighbour to the north.
Harbour Commissions Act
In this day of growing government and government involvement more and more in the private affairs of people, it seems to me there is an increasing need to broaden representation on commissions such as the one at issue at the moment. The basis of the amendment proposed by the hon. member is to increase the number of commissioners from three to five. He has suggested a number of amendments to the act which I think are most appropriate.
There is no harbour commission within my constituency, but there is one in the neighbouring constituency to the south, the riding of Victoria. There is, of course, a harbour commission in that city with powers which extend to the inner harbour. I have had some experience with smaller harbours within my constituency and know something of the problems encountered by the municipality and people living in the area. First of all, and this happened only about a month ago, an attempt was made by the municipality in which the harbour, or bay, was located to conclude a lease over a wharf in the harbour to be used for multiple purposes. Basically, it is a federal wharf. This question involves the Government Harbours and Piers Act because these are related acts. This is a government wharf provided for the community. Many people living in the community of Sidney, at the north end of the Saanich peninsula, are fishermen; but in that area there is also a great tourist industry.
We receive many sports craft from Vancouver, from further up the inland passage and, of course, from our neighbour to the south, coming up through Puget Sound, the Strait of Georgia, Hecate Strait and beyond. Frequently they occupy wharf space in this area. The municipality was anxious to ensure that prime space at this wharf was accorded those who live in the community and for whom this facility had been provided.
The community ran up against a snag in concluding the lease, in not being sure that the wharf engineer, who is appointed by the Minister of Transport, had the power to conclude the lease or whether he just had the power to collect the parking fees, if you like, at the wharf. They wanted more than that; they wanted to apply more regulations than were actually applied and they wanted to be sure that the wharf engineer would have the power to apply them.
I believe it was a question of misunderstanding, which I was able to help clear up. Now I believe it will work satisfactorily. The fishermen who live in that area will have the pride of having representation on the board. The sportsmen in the area will be able to come to the wharf. They must pay their fees. I gather the fees previously had been collected rather indefinitely for a time. This emphasizes to everybody in that small inlet the need even for fishermen, perhaps, to be represented on commissions in the case of a fishermen's harbour.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) mentioned environmentalists. It seems to me that the act he criticized, I suppose just through the passage of time, has failed to take into account some of the new interests and concerns of the Canadian people. When fishermen or sportsmen come alongside, there is a tenden-

April 13, 1973
Harbour Commissions Act
cy to pump out the bilges of their boats and to throw out their garbage. This should not occur. The commission should have the power to prevent it occurring.
It seems to me there is a real problem and there should be on the board the representative of an environmental interest, be it a local representative of the Department of the Environment or a local body concerned with the environment, to ensure that the law is properly observed and that the harbour is kept in proper order and clean for the public. Perhaps one of the members should be drawn from marina operators, sportsmen or harbour people, depending on the use to which the particular harbour, bay or wharf is devoted.
Sometimes representatives of tourism, if you like, representatives of fishermen and of environmental interests have their part to play in the commissions which are established. I note, for example, that the law as it now stands makes provision for the council to have a representative on the commission. I quite agree that the citizens of these communities ought to be represented. However, there is also the question of functional representation about which I have made a plea.
There is another example in an area which to some extent is a boundary link between my constituency and the constituency of Victoria. It is known in Victoria as "the gorge". It is a long, deep inlet of the sea. It is subject to the tides. It brings pollution from the sea into the narrows. There is a narrows through which one must travel; it is barely half the width of this room. There was a time when people could swim in the gorge. That time has now passed. I have asked people why it is that they no longer swim there. The obvious answer is, because of pollution from industries that have been established around the port of Victoria. This matter is being dealt with. The municipality and the harbour commission are working hand in hand, sometimes in the same direction and sometimes in conflict.
I agree that there should be greater provision in the act for regular consultation and also community consultation. The other matter in respect of the gorge is that some of the effluent is carried out to sea. The people who towed me through the gorge are a constituted group concerned with restoring the gorge to its earlier purity. People of this type would be happy to serve on the commission. They told me about the conflict in respect of jurisdiction between the province, the municipality and the federal authorities. How far up into the gorge does the federal authority extend? This has never been very clear. Should the day ever come when Esquimalt harbour could receive civil ships, it would deserve to come under a jurisdiction with
the broadest possible base of consultation. Today, however, it is under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence.
I am happy, Mr. Speaker, to support the purpose of the bill to increase the number of commissioners on the Nanaimo Harbour Commission, because it leads the way to further developments, to another study of the basic act so that it might be broadened to take into account the new interests, the new concerns and the new worries of our people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE THAT REPRESENTATIVE OF MUNICIPALITIES SERVE ON NANAIMO HARBOUR COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like, through you, to say it is always a pleasure to listen to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). I agree wholeheartedly with the comments he made pertaining to possible amendments to the Harbour Commissions Act. I believe this is a matter of concern not only to that area but other areas. If a change is to be made, and I hope it will, it should include all harbour commissions across our nation; it should embrace them all.
Several hon. members have indicated their interest in this particular field. I could possibly name several but I shall not do so. I am tempted to do so, however. Instead, I will say that the government has no objection to the hon. member's Bill C-21, which primarily is concerned with the administration of the Nanaimo Harbour Commission. We feel, however, that this bill should be recognized by the House as an interim measure. We feel it should be an interim measure because the National Ports Council, which includes representation from the harbour commissions, the National Harbours Board and all the provinces, is now reviewing the structure of all Canadian ports and harbours with a view to making recommendations on new, streamlined mechanisms for the administration of these facilities. We think it is vital to have an input from the provinces and these organizations, and because of this the House should recognize the necessity of this bill being only an interim measure.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
